news_drafts.headline: Aberdeenshire health partnership stabilises finances with £19m savings, but gains rest on one-off measures
news_drafts.lead: Aberdeenshire's health and social care partnership delivered £19 million of savings in 2025/26 and moved to break-even after years of deficit, the council's annual performance report shows. About 70 per cent of the savings are recurring. However, the council's own budget risk register states the improved position rests entirely on non-recurring factors — reserves, temporary grants and vacancy management — rather than sustainable change. The structural budget gap, where recurring spending exceeds recurring funding, remains unresolved. The partnership's medium-term financial strategy forecasts a £66 million deficit by 2030/31. Separately, five national indicators of health and social care quality — ability to live independently, having a say in care, service coordination, GP experience and feeling safe — now perform more than 5 per cent below the Scottish average, all rated red. Demand for crisis mental health support rose 64 per cent year-on-year.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership Annual Performance Report 2025-2026

news_drafts.headline: Aberdeenshire closes in-year budget gap with temporary savings; structural deficit unresolved
news_drafts.lead: Aberdeenshire Council stabilised its 2025/26 budget after years of overspend, with its health and social care partnership delivering £19m of savings, about 70% of them recurring. The council's own risk register, however, identifies a structural budget gap that persists: recurring expenditure exceeds sustainable funding, and the underlying position has not improved. The apparent gain this year and into 2026/27 came from one-off funding, reserves and vacancy management, not from closing the structural mismatch. The integration joint board forecasts a deficit of £66.2m by 2030/31, which will fall to the council and NHS to address. Meanwhile, five national indicators of health and social care experience have fallen more than 5% below the Scottish average since 2023/24, including ability to live independently, having a say in care, and service coordination. The council says the pace of financial recovery depends on timely decisions to redirect resources to areas of greatest strategic importance and demographic pressure. Capital plans are also under pressure; services are managing rising construction costs and borrowing charges almost entirely by reducing scope, deferring maintenance and reprofiling works to later years.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Aberdeenshire Health and Social Care Partnership Annual Performance Report 2025-2026

news_drafts.headline: Aberdeenshire's health partnership delivers £19m savings but underlying budget gap remains unresolved
news_drafts.lead: Aberdeenshire's health and social care partnership delivered £19 million of savings in 2025/26, stabilising its position after years of chronic overspend. About 70 per cent of the savings are recurring, the partnership reported to the council. However, the council's own budget papers make clear that this improvement, and the favourable outturn for 2025/26, have been achieved through non-recurring factors — reserves, one-off savings and temporary grants — rather than through changes to the underlying structure of spending and funding. The structural budget gap persists. At the same time, five national health and social care indicators have fallen more than 5 per cent below the Scottish average, all rated red. These include the proportion of people able to live independently (67.8 per cent against Scotland's 73.6 per cent) and those having a say in care (55.9 per cent against 63.9 per cent). The partnership's medium-term financial strategy forecasts a deficit of £66.2 million by 2030/31.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges that delivering climate commitments requires 'significant Capital investment' for which it may lack long-term funding
findings.detail: The risk assessment explicitly identifies that budget pressures can only be mitigated if additional long-term funding becomes available for capital investment. This signals the council has committed to capital spending on climate change that it cannot currently fund.
findings.matters: Signals potential future borrowing requirement or budget reallocation if the council is to deliver on its stated climate change capital programme
findings.quote: Budget pressures can only be mitigated against if additional sufficient long term funding is made available to support the significant Capital investment required to meet climate change targets.

findings.headline: Environment and Infrastructure Services cuts planned emissions reductions by 69% as LED streetlighting project receives no capital funding allocation
findings.detail: The service's estimated emissions reductions dropped from 81 tCO2e to 25 tCO2e for 2026/27. The council explicitly identifies the lack of capital funding for LED streetlighting rollout as the primary reason for this reduction.
findings.matters: Demonstrates capital budget constraints preventing delivery of planned infrastructure projects, with the council having to scale back its own emissions reduction commitments
findings.figures: estimated reduction in emissions from projects has decreased from 81 tCO2e to 25 tCO2e
findings.quote: The main reduction has been due to the impact of no capital funding being allocated to the continued rollout of LED streetlighting for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - External Auditor’s Draft Annual Audit Report to the Board 2025/ 26
findings.headline: Balance sheet omitted from draft financial statements; related party disclosures materially restated during audit (NHS income increased £17.763m; payments increased £4.032m)
findings.detail: The draft accounts submitted for audit omitted the balance sheet entirely. Additionally, the related party transactions note required material amendment during audit: NHS Grampian income was restated upward by £17.763m and payments upward by £4.032m. Auditors have recommended that the IJB implement formal quality assurance review of annual accounts before submission, indicating control weaknesses in the accounting function.
findings.matters: Omission of a primary statement and material audit amendments suggest control weaknesses; a lender needs confidence in the reliability of financial reporting and the strength of the control environment.
findings.figures: Balance sheet omitted (corrected in audit); NHS Grampian income restated up £17.763m; payments restated up £4.032m
findings.quote: One primary statement issue was noted as a balance sheet had been omitted from the draft financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - External Auditor’s Draft Annual Audit Report to the Board 2025/ 26
findings.headline: Apparent reserves increase to £11.735m is entirely driven by one-off £8.002m transfer from NHS Grampian, with £7.6m already planned to be drawn down in 2026/27
findings.detail: The IJB reported general reserves of £8.002m at 31 March 2026, a dramatic increase from zero. This resulted entirely from NHS Grampian transferring its unused underwritten funding, not from the IJB reducing its structural deficit. The approved 2026/27 budget assumes draw-down of £7.6m of this £8.002m to address the funding gap. The apparent reserves improvement is temporary and will be largely consumed within 12 months.
findings.matters: A lender must distinguish between structural reserves (demonstrating prudence) and temporary funding transfers (one-time cash injections); this masks continued underlying weakness and provides no resilience.
findings.figures: £8.002m general reserves (one-off transfer); £7.6m planned draw-down 2026/27; £11.735m total reported reserves
findings.quote: The approved 2026/27 budget assumes the utilisation of £7.6 million of these general reserves to support service delivery and address the budget gap during the year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - External Auditor’s Draft Annual Audit Report to the Board 2025/ 26
findings.headline: £1.493m of £5.718m required 2026/27 savings assessed as likely to deliver; £4.209m rated at risk
findings.detail: At Q1 2026/27 (end June 2026), just 26% of required savings are forecast as likely to be achieved. The remaining 74% are rated amber or red, indicating serious delivery risk. The Senior Leadership Team is working to identify alternative savings proposals, implying the current plans lack credibility. This mirrors 2025/26 when 40% of planned savings were not achieved and required partner bailout.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver these savings will trigger emergency partner funding for a second consecutive year, establishing an unsustainable financing pattern.
findings.quote: At the end of June 2026, the IJB were predicting: - Expect to achieve £1.493 million of savings (rated green) - £4.209 million of savings are at risk of not being achieved (rated amber or red).

daily_post.headline: Council identifies £1.45m potential additional energy cost pressure in 2026/27 despite Q1 position on budget
daily_post.lead: Energy costs are volatile and council-wide. If the £1.45m potential pressure materializes, it would erode approximately one-third of the current Q1 underspend and reinforce reliance on reserves or further service cuts.
